title: How to make a great video with an AI agent
excerpt: Five principles for getting better results from AI video agents: set the goal and audience, bring your source material, say what viewers should do next, describe the look in plain words, and treat the first version as a draft. Includes three example prompts.
content_html:
Today, anyone can describe a video in a sentence and get a finished one back from an AI video agent. Getting a good one still comes down to two things: knowing how to ask for it, and having a creative idea worth asking for.

If you run a small business or a small team, AI video agents are good news. You don’t need an editor, a designer or a big budget. You just need a clear message and some principles on how to make it work. Five principles make the biggest difference to what comes back after the prompt: set the goal and audience, bring your source material, say what viewers should do next, describe the look and feel in plain words, and treat the first version as a draft.

1. Start with the dials

Start by setting the dials before you type anything, including the goal, audience and scope. The goal is what the video should achieve. The audience is who watches and what they already know. The scope is how long the video runs, how many topics it covers and how long each scene lasts. Favor a story arc over an infodump, with a problem, a tension and a resolution. When you write the prompt, describe it conversationally, like a mood board in words.

2. Bring what you already have

Most people have more raw material than they think. Give the agent the material you already have instead of asking it to guess. Good sources include a help-center article, a PDF manual, a slide deck, a product page or a launch blog post. The agent applies your brand guidelines, terminology and product details to the video, so you spend less time correcting facts afterwards.

3. Say who it’s for and what you want them to do

Name the viewer and the action you want them to take. A video for a new hire and a video for a prospective customer should look and sound different, even when the facts are identical. State the next step, whether that is a sign-up, a booked call, a set of steps to follow or one thing to remember. The type of video also shapes the brief:

  • Brand films should chase emotion and originality over completeness.
  • Product explainers should lead with the problem and treat features as the means of solving it.
  • Internal comms should be clear and honest, with no spin.
  • Social videos live or die on the first second, so say that in the prompt.

4. Describe the look and feel in plain words

Use plain words, not design vocabulary. “Clean and calm, with lots of white space” or “upbeat and fast-paced, like a product launch” is enough to steer the result. A good place to add reassurance: if you can’t describe it in words, upload images that match the look and feel of what you’re going for. Share your brand colors, logo or past videos you like if you have them. Before you had a mood board in words but you can actually attach a mood board in images too. Business video has to look like your business, not like a generic template, and an AI video agent can only match a style it has seen.

5. Treat the first version as a draft

Treat the first version as a draft and keep talking to the agent. The real advantage of working with an agent is that you can revise by conversation: “Make the opening shorter.” “Swap the second scene for a screenshot of the dashboard.” “Make the tone warmer.” Small, specific requests work better than “make it better.” Change one or two things at a time so you can see what each change did, and stop when the video says what you wanted to say.

Example prompts for AI video agents

These three prompts come from our team and apply all five principles. Replace the bracketed text with your own details.

  • Product launch announcement (marketing) – Create a 45 second launch video for [product], aimed at [audience, e.g. IT directors at mid-size companies]. Open with the problem they face today: [one sentence]. Then show the product solving it, using the attached screenshots. End with one call to action: book a demo at [URL]. Confident and energetic, fast cuts, no more than three features. Use the attached deck for brand look and feel.
  • Executive or all-hands update (internal comms) – Create a 90 second update for all employees on [topic, e.g. our Q4 priorities], based on the attached memo. Be clear and honest, with no spin. Cover three points only: what’s changing, why, and what it means for each team. Calm, steady pacing with room to breathe. Warm, direct tone.
  • Webinar or event promo (social) – Make a 20 second vertical teaser for our webinar on [topic] on [date]. Hook the viewer in the first second with the most surprising stat from the attached slides. Fast pacing, bold on-screen text, upbeat music. End with “Register free” and the link.

Five videos to try first

If you’re not sure where to start, these are the videos most small teams have been meaning to make and now can:

  • A 60-second explainer of what you do, for your homepage and YouTube
  • A how-to that answers the questions customers ask most
  • An onboarding walkthrough for new customers or new hires
  • An announcement for a new feature, offer or service
  • A video version of your best blog post or FAQ page

Where should you start?

Pick the one video on the list above that you have been putting off and make it today. Try it with Synthesia Syren, the AI video generator for business. It works like a video agent: you start from a prompt or your own documents, it builds the video with your brand, and you refine it by chatting.

Syren runs as a web app and inside ChatGPT and Claude, so you can start wherever you already work.

Making video is becoming a basic work skill, like writing a clear email or building a PowerPoint deck. The people who get good at it know exactly what they want to say and what they want viewers to do once they have said it.
